intro: Right now, while you read this, your heart is beating. Your lungs are filling with air. Your stomach may be working on your last meal. Your brain is turning these letters into ideas. You do not have to tell any of these parts what to do. They work on their own, and they work together.

In this unit you will explore the main systems of the body: bones and muscles, the heart and blood, the lungs, digestion, the brain and nerves, and the skin. Then you will learn how food gives these systems the fuel and building blocks they need. You will see healthy meals from many parts of the world.

By the end, you will be able to name the body's main systems and explain how they team up. You will be able to read a food label, use MyPlate and plan a balanced meal. You will also be able to explain why no single food is 'bad,' and why balance and variety help.
bigQuestion: How do the body's systems work together, and how does food help them do their jobs?

timeline.t: Andreas Vesalius publishes careful drawings of the human body, based on his own study.
William Harvey shows that the heart pumps blood around the body in a loop.
James Lind reports his test showing oranges and lemons help sailors with scurvy.
René Laennec invents the stethoscope to listen to the heart and lungs.
Wilhelm Röntgen discovers X-rays, letting doctors see bones inside the body.
Casimir Funk uses the word 'vitamine' for nutrients needed in small amounts.
Grand Rapids, Michigan, becomes the first U.S. city to add fluoride to its water.
The U.S. National School Lunch Program begins.
The Nutrition Facts label becomes required on most U.S. packaged foods.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture introduces MyPlate.

test.q: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
test.why: The heart is a muscle that pumps blood through the blood vessels.

test.q: What is the largest organ of the body?
test.why: Skin is the largest organ. It protects you and helps keep you cool.

test.q: Which gas do you breathe out as waste?
test.why: The lungs take in oxygen and send out carbon dioxide.

test.q: What ties a muscle to a bone?
test.why: Tendons are strong cords that tie muscles to bones.

test.q: Which body system includes the brain, spinal cord and nerves?
test.why: The brain, spinal cord and nerves carry messages. They form the nervous system.

test.q: When you run, why do you breathe faster?
choices: To bring in more oxygen for your muscles
test.why: Working muscles need more oxygen, so the lungs and heart speed up together.

test.q: Where are most useful parts of food taken into the blood?
test.why: The small intestine is a long, folded tube where food parts pass into the blood.

test.q: Which nutrient is needed in small amounts and was missing for James Lind's sailors?
test.why: Oranges and lemons helped the sailors. They have vitamin C.

test.q: Which food is a good source of calcium?
test.why: Calcium is found in milk, yogurt, tofu and leafy greens. It builds bones and teeth.

test.q: On MyPlate, what does the small cup stand for?
test.why: The cup beside the MyPlate stands for dairy, like milk or yogurt, or fortified soy milk.

test.q: On a food label, 20 percent Daily Value of a nutrient is usually thought of as...
test.why: As a rough guide, 5 percent is low and 20 percent is high.

test.q: How do germs in the mouth cause cavities?
choices: They use sugar to make acid
test.why: Germs eat sugar and make acid. The acid can make holes in teeth.

test.q: Which meal gives a grain, a protein and a vegetable?
choices: Rice, lentil dal and cooked spinach
test.why: Rice is a grain, lentil dal gives protein and spinach is a vegetable.

choices: That food is digested in the brain
That blood circulates in a loop
test.why: In 1628 Harvey showed that the heart pumps the same blood around the body again and again.

test.q: What does this unit say about 'bad' foods?
choices: Only foods from one country are healthy
No single food is bad; balance and variety matter most
Sweets should be eaten at every meal
test.why: The unit teaches balance and variety. A treat now and then fits in a healthy week.

write.prompt: A friend says, "Food only matters for your stomach." Do you agree? Write a paragraph that answers the question. Use two or three facts from this unit about how food helps other body systems, like muscles, bones, blood or teeth.
tips: Start with a clear sentence that says what you think.
Name at least two nutrients and the body parts they help.
Use unit words, like nutrients, circulation or muscle.
Name where a fact came from, like MyPlate or James Lind's test.
End by telling your friend what helps: balance and variety.
